title: Yorkshire Parkin
subtitle: sticky oat-and-treacle traybake for Bonfire Night
excerpt: Yorkshire parkin is a dense, sticky oat cake made with black treacle and golden syrup. It keeps well and actually improves over a few days in a tin, making it ideal for baking ahead of Bonfire Night. Serves 16 squares.
sourceNotes: Yorkshire parkin is one of the oldest regional British cakes, associated specifically with Bonfire Night (5 November) and the wider Guy Fawkes tradition. Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861, Project Gutenberg #10136) gives a parkin recipe based on oatmeal and treacle. Hannah Glasse, The Art of Cookery (1747, Project Gutenberg), includes a gingerbread of similar character. The name is thought to be northern dialect for a form of gingerbread; the oatmeal base distinguishes Yorkshire parkin from its Lancashire cousin. The essential test of a good parkin is stickiness: freshly baked it is crumbly; given two or three days in an airtight tin it softens and becomes properly tacky.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cut squares in a single layer, then stack with baking parchment between them. Thaw overnight at room temperature.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make parkin two to three days before eating. It is noticeably stickier and better after resting in an airtight tin.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thick, dark, very strongly flavoured molasses-based syrup used in British baking. Stickier and more bitter than golden syrup. Called molasses in North America.

content.text: Yorkshire parkin is a heavy, moist traybake made with oatmeal,

, and ginger. The day it comes out of the oven it cuts cleanly but has a slightly firm crumb. Leave it in a tin for two or three days and the texture changes: it softens right through and becomes properly sticky, which is the real point. Bonfire Night is its occasion, but a tin of parkin is good company all through autumn.

The bake is simple: melt the fat and syrups together, stir in the dry ingredients, pour into a lined tin. The one variable to manage is oven temperature. Parkin needs a slow, steady heat, 160°C fan, to cook through without scorching the top. A tin-foil lid for the last ten minutes prevents darkening while the centre sets.

items.prepNote: medium oatmeal or blended porridge oats

content.text: You need a 20 cm x 30 cm rectangular baking tin, lined with baking parchment. A large saucepan is easier than a heatproof bowl for melting the syrups and butter together.
Prepare the tin and mix the dry ingredients
Heat the oven to 160°C fan (180°C conventional). Line a 20 cm x 30 cm tin with baking parchment, pushing it into the corners.

Put {{porridge-oats}} of oatmeal, {{plain-flour}} of flour, {{dark-brown-sugar}} of dark brown sugar, {{ginger-ground}} of ground ginger, and {{cinnamon-ground}} of cinnamon into a large bowl. Add {{baking-powder}} of baking powder, {{bicarbonate-of-soda}} of bicarbonate of soda, and {{salt-table}} of salt. Stir until combined.

Put {{black-treacle}} of black treacle, {{golden-syrup}} of golden syrup, and {{unsalted-butter}} of butter into a saucepan. Warm over a low heat, stirring, until the butter melts and everything is liquid. Do not boil.
Take the pan off the heat. Stir in {{whole-milk}} of milk and the beaten egg. Pour onto the dry ingredients and stir until the batter is smooth and even. It will be quite thin.
Pour the batter into the prepared tin and spread level. Bake for 35 to 40 minutes. After 30 minutes, lay a sheet of foil loosely over the top to prevent darkening.
The parkin is done when a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean and the edges have pulled slightly from the tin. Leave to cool completely in the tin before cutting into squares.
Transfer to an airtight tin and leave for at least two days before eating. The parkin improves markedly.

items.symptom: Parkin sinks in the middle after cooling
items.cause: Underbaked, or oven temperature too high causing the edges to set before the centre
items.fix: Use an oven thermometer to verify temperature. Give it another 5 minutes and test with a skewer.

items.symptom: Top burns before the centre is cooked
items.cause: Oven runs hot, or foil cover not placed early enough
items.fix: Cover with foil from the 25-minute mark and reduce temperature by 10°C.

items.symptom: Parkin stays dry and crumbly after resting
items.cause: Too much flour relative to oats, or stored in a paper bag rather than an airtight tin
items.fix: Always store in a metal tin with a tight lid. The parkin needs to retain its moisture as it rests.

items.cause: Treacle proportion too high, or treacle is old and has oxidised
items.fix: Use fresh black treacle. The ratio of treacle to golden syrup matters; the golden syrup softens the treacle's sharpness.

content.text: Parkin belongs to the 5th of November. In Yorkshire it goes with bonfire toffee and hot drinks after the fireworks, and the tin tends to sit on a kitchen counter all week as people cut squares whenever they pass. It is one of the few British cakes that rewards patience: cutting into it on the day it was baked is always a slight disappointment, but three days later it is exactly as it should be. There is a Lancashire version too, but it uses less oatmeal and a different syrup balance. Yorkshire parkin insists on the oatmeal; the texture comes from nothing else.
